photos.title: The Euphrates River From Space
photos.caption: Dark green irrigated farms hug the riverbanks while dry tan desert begins just past the canals.

photos.title: Close-Up of a Barley Stalk
photos.caption: Each bristled head packs rows of barley seeds—irrigated Sumerian plots harvested 15 to 30 grains per seed planted.

photos.title: Real Beveled-Rim Bowl (c. 3200–3000 BCE)
photos.caption: Coarse, mold-pressed clay (~0.8–1 liter); thousands were discarded near early Mesopotamian temples and canals over 5,000 years ago.

photos.title: Proto-Cuneiform Barley & Malt Tablet (c. 3100 BCE)
photos.caption: Pressed reed circles and wedges track malted barley and groats on sun-dried river clay—more than 5,000 years ago.
photos.credit: Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access (CC0)

photos.title: The Real Ziggurat of Ur Today
photos.caption: Notice the sloped buttressed baked-brick walls, small dark square weep-holes on the left, and tiny visitors on top for scale.

photos.title: Date Palms Along the Euphrates
photos.caption: Southern banks offered mud, marsh reeds, and spongy date palms—almost no building stone or strong roof timber.

photos.title: Raw Afghan Lapis Lazuli Stone
photos.caption: Deep-blue stone from Afghanistan imported by Sumerian traders and paid for with exported woven wool cloth.
photos.credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

photos.title: Sealed Clay Contract Envelope (c. 2100–2000 BCE)
photos.caption: Witnesses rolled a stone cylinder seal across this wet outer clay shell—about 4,000 years ago—to lock the contract tablet sealed inside.
photos.credit: Harvard Semitic Museum / Wikimedia Commons (Public Domain)

photos.title: White Mineral Salt Wicking Out of Soil
photos.caption: When fierce heat evaporates trapped salty groundwater, white mineral salt crusts the topsoil—and even climbs halfway up a dry wooden fence post like water wicking into a sponge.
